football_evidence.question: Can Utah stop Cincinnati’s run game?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Utah, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.0 of the 3.0 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Cincinnati has the ball (big plays through the air): Cincinnati’s offense turns 7.6% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Utah’s defense gives up explosive gains on 9.1% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When Cincinnati has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Cincinnati’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 16.1% of its runs, and Utah’s defense stops 22.3% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
When Utah has the ball (third down): Utah’s offense converts 52.9% of its third downs, and Cincinnati’s defense allows opponents to convert 43.1% of their third downs (FBS average 39.5%).

When Utah has the ball (down-to-down efficiency): Utah’s offense succeeds on 51.0% of its offensive plays, and Cincinnati’s defense allows opponents to succeed on 44.6% of their plays (FBS average 42.3%).
contradicting: In his last two games (Kansas and Colorado), Dampier averaged 7.2 yards per attempt, against 9.0 in his four games before that.
In his last two games (Utah State and Kansas), Ficklin averaged 8.8 yards per attempt, against 11.1 in his two games before that.
When Cincinnati has the ball (the red zone): Cincinnati’s offense succeeds on 58.5% of its red-zone plays, and Utah’s defense allows success on 40.2% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.6%).
